videoIdeas.title: How to not freeze when everyone's looking at you
videoIdeas.hook: You don't have a public speaking problem. You have a preparation problem.
videoIdeas.rationale: Birdtart's networking-tactic video hit 2M views and doctordaanish's '20s advice, save this' lists are pulling 60k+. Practical, save-able 'how to' content is winning right now. I post almost no tactical public speaking content — this is my biggest gap in a pillar I'm supposed to own.
videoIdeas.script:
You don't have a public speaking problem. You have a preparation problem.

Everyone who's ever frozen on stage told themselves the same lie: 'I'll figure out what to say when I'm up there.' You won't. Your brain doesn't improvise under pressure. It panics.

So do this. Know your first line cold. Not the whole speech — the first line. The reason people blank is the opening, not the middle. Once your mouth starts moving, the rest follows.

Second: slow down on purpose. Everyone speeds up when nervous. If you force one deliberate pause, the room reads it as confidence. They don't know you're just breathing.

Confidence isn't a personality. It's reps plus a plan. Get both.

visuals.setting: Standing, mid-shot, plain wall or empty hall that looks like a venue. Smart casual — neutral colours. Calm, controlled energy, not hyped. Talk straight into the lens like you're correcting one person.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'You don't have a public speaking problem' appears while you hold a beat of silence before speaking — the delay forces the viewer to wait.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-pause: start frozen, eyes wide, then break into the line
On-screen text punchline that corrects itself: 'public speaking problem' crosses out, 'preparation problem' replaces it
Count up a '3-second pause' on screen to visually demonstrate the deliberate pause tip

videoIdeas.title: The leader everyone actually follows isn't the loudest one
videoIdeas.hook: The loudest person in the room is almost never the leader.
videoIdeas.rationale: My account under-indexes on tactical leadership despite it being a core pillar. Lifeofdinoo proves short, two-sided truth statements ('You can pray and still need help. Both can be true.') travel far. A contrarian leadership take in that same tight format fits my blunt voice and fills a gap.
videoIdeas.script:
The loudest person in the room is almost never the leader.

We grew up thinking leadership is volume. Command the room, raise your voice, take up space. So young brothers perform confidence instead of building it.

Real authority is quieter than that. It's the person everyone looks at when something goes wrong. Not because he shouted — because he's reliable. People follow certainty, not noise.

You want to lead? Be the one who keeps his word when it's inconvenient. Be the one who stays calm when the room heats up. Do that for six months and people hand you the room without you asking.

Volume gets attention. Consistency gets followed.

visuals.setting: Seated, slightly closer framing, softer light. Darker neutral top. Measured, lower-energy delivery to match the message about quiet authority.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'the loudest ≠ the leader' with you speaking very quietly, almost leaning in — the low volume reinforces the point.
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: open on an exaggerated loud gesture, then drop to stillness and lower your voice
Two-line on-screen text that mirrors the lifeofdinoo 'both can be true' structure
Cold open on the word 'Wrong.' before the hook line

videoIdeas.title: Being in the room is the whole point
videoIdeas.hook: I'm not the fastest runner in the room. I stopped caring about that two years ago.
videoIdeas.rationale: My running video ('Might not be the fastest in the room. But I am in the room') is my single best-performing post at 2,658 views. That exact framing is proven with my audience. I should extend it into a full mindset piece instead of leaving it as a one-line caption.
videoIdeas.script:
I'm not the fastest runner in the room. I stopped caring about that two years ago.

Here's what nobody tells you about being around people better than you: it's supposed to feel uncomfortable. If you're the best one in every room you walk into, you've chosen the wrong rooms.

Most people quit the moment they feel behind. They confuse being behind with not belonging. Those are not the same thing.

You don't earn your place by being the best. You earn it by still showing up when you're clearly not. The fast ones who stayed home learned nothing today. You did.

Might not be the fastest. But I'm in the room. Stay in the room.

visuals.setting: Shot outdoors mid-run or right after — slightly out of breath, real, not polished. Running gear. Raw and honest energy, the opposite of a studio motivational clip.
visuals.visualHook: Cold open mid-run, breathing hard, on-screen text 'not the fastest in the room' — the physical exhaustion is the hook.
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: freeze-frame on you getting overtaken by faster runners, text 'this used to break me'
Open on the finish-line or empty track, then cut to you
On-screen text punchline 'in the room' lands on a hard cut to stillness

videoIdeas.title: Stop saying 'um' — here's the actual fix
videoIdeas.hook: 'Um' isn't a bad habit. It's a thinking-out-loud habit. Here's how to kill it.
videoIdeas.rationale: Save-able, specific 'how to' tactics are the format winning across my competitors right now (birdtart's networking questions, doctordaanish's journaling). A micro-skill breakdown in public speaking is tactical, shareable, and something none of my competitors in the Muslim self-dev space are doing well.
videoIdeas.script:
'Um' isn't a bad habit. It's a thinking-out-loud habit. And there's one fix.

People say 'um' because they're scared of silence. Your brain hasn't finished the sentence, so you fill the gap with noise so nobody thinks you've stopped.

But here's the thing — silence sounds confident to everyone except you. When you pause, the listener thinks you're choosing your words. When you say 'um', they think you don't have any.

So replace the 'um' with a closed mouth. That's it. Finish a sentence, shut your mouth, let the pause sit, then start the next one. Feels like forever to you. Feels like authority to them.

Record yourself for one week. Count the ums. Watch them drop.

visuals.setting: Clean mid-shot, bright, talking head. Smart casual. Crisp, instructive energy — you're teaching, not preaching. Could use a subtle on-screen counter.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen 'um' counter ticking up next to your head, then it freezes and the text changes to 'the fix:' — visual demonstration of the problem.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open with you deliberately saying a sentence full of 'ums', then stopping to say 'notice that?'
On-screen text punchline: 'silence = confidence' appears during an actual held pause
Caption-style subtitles that remove the 'um' live on screen

videoIdeas.title: Andalusia didn't fall because of outside enemies
videoIdeas.hook: Muslims ruled Spain for 700 years. They didn't lose it to a stronger army. They lost it to themselves.
videoIdeas.rationale: My Tariq bin Ziyad / Andalusia post pulled 1,640 views — strong reach — but only 33 likes, meaning the history grabbed attention but the framing didn't land a lesson people wanted to engage with. Reframing history into a sharp leadership lesson (why disunity kills) keeps the reach but gives people a reason to react and share.
videoIdeas.script:
Muslims ruled Spain for nearly 700 years. They didn't lose it to a stronger army. They lost it to themselves.

Andalusia didn't collapse in a day. It rotted from the inside. The one empire split into dozens of tiny kingdoms, each ruler more obsessed with his own throne than the bigger picture. Taifa against taifa. Brother against brother.

They were so busy competing with each other that they invited outside powers in to settle their petty scores. Those powers never left.

Here's the lesson, and it's not just history. Any group — a team, a community, an ummah — doesn't get destroyed by the enemy outside. It gets destroyed by the ego inside. Division does what no army could.

Unity isn't soft. It's survival.

visuals.setting: Seated, serious tone, slightly moodier lighting. Could overlay archival images or Alhambra footage as b-roll. Lower, deliberate delivery — a storyteller, not a hype account.
visuals.visualHook: Full-screen image of the Alhambra with on-screen text '700 years. Lost from the inside.' before cutting to you.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on a map of Al-Andalus splintering into pieces
On-screen text punchline 'the enemy was inside' on a hard cut
Start mid-sentence on 'they lost it to themselves' then rewind to explain

videoIdeas.title: Speaking up for someone costs you something — do it anyway
videoIdeas.hook: Speaking out for the oppressed is easy when there's no cost. The test is when there is one.
videoIdeas.rationale: My Majid Freeman post got 289 likes — my highest like count in the dataset — showing my audience responds strongly to principled, justice-driven content. Saffana's activism posts dominate her reach for the same reason. This leans into proven territory for my audience but reframes it around personal courage so it's not a one-off news post.
videoIdeas.script:
Speaking out for the oppressed is easy when there's no cost. The test is when there is one.

Everyone's brave in the group chat. Everyone's got an opinion when it's safe and the crowd already agrees. That's not courage. That's following.

The Prophet ﷺ said whoever sees an injustice should change it with his hand, or his tongue, or his heart. Notice the order. The hand first. Action before words. Words before quiet disapproval. The bare minimum is to at least hate it in your heart — and that's described as the weakest of faith.

So ask yourself honestly: when speaking up might actually cost you — a friendship, a job, your reputation — do you still open your mouth?

If the answer is only yes when it's free, it was never conviction. It was convenience.

visuals.setting: Direct, still, closer framing. Plain background. Calm but weighty delivery — no shouting, let the words carry. Serious tone.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'easy when it's free' holds in silence for a beat before you start — makes the viewer sit with it.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on the single word 'Convenience.' then build back
On-screen text laying out the hand/tongue/heart hierarchy as you say it
Pattern interrupt: start with 'Everyone's brave in the group chat' as a dismissive line

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your best post — 2,658 views, 122 likes, 12 comments. The caption 'Might not be the fastest in the room. But I am in the room' is your voice at its sharpest: short, two-sided, no filler, and it reframes a physical struggle into a mindset win. The running b-roll gives it an honest, non-studio feel people trust.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: You left the best idea in the caption instead of the video. That one line is a full mindset piece. Turn it into a spoken script and put the framing on screen in the first 3 seconds, so the hook works even on mute. Also the hashtags (#running #halfmarathoner) pull a fitness crowd, not your self-dev audience — swap for intent-based framing in the caption.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Strong reach — 1,640 views — which proves the Islamic history angle grabs attention and distribution. The Tariq bin Ziyad opening line is vivid and specific; concrete history outperforms vague inspiration.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 1,640 views but only 33 likes and 0 comments is a signal: people watched but had no reason to react. History alone isn't enough — it needs a lesson they can apply to themselves today. Reframe it so the last line hands the viewer a leadership takeaway (division kills from the inside) and ends on a question or a challenge that invites comments.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 1,538 views on a light, personal, funny post ('Never running through a park at night ever again 😭'). This shows your audience rewards personality and relatability, not just lessons. Humour and a real moment travel.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: It's pure entertainment with no bridge back to your pillars, so the reach doesn't build your positioning. Keep the funny hook but land a one-line mindset tie-in at the end — turn the scare into a point about discomfort or showing up anyway. Let personality be the hook, not the whole payload.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Clear, relatable problem in the first line ('Burnout affects so many of us') and a specific solution. Naming a real pain point your medical-student-adjacent audience feels is smart targeting.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 701 views is your lowest performer here, and the caption reads like a product pitch for the Sabr app rather than your voice. Promo content suppresses reach when it leads with the product. Lead with the burnout truth as a standalone value piece in your blunt voice, earn the attention, and only mention the tool at the very end — or in a comment.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 289 likes — your highest like count in the set. Principled, justice-driven content clearly resonates most with your audience, and leading with the hadith on changing injustice fits your voice and values perfectly. This is proven territory.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: It's a Sidecar (image carousel) with no view count — your audience is clearly video-first, and every top post across you and your competitors is video. Rebuild this kind of principled message as a talking-head reel so it gets reach, not just likes from existing followers. Also broaden one version from a single news event to the timeless principle (speaking up when it costs you) so it stays relevant beyond the moment.
